script.base: Spread and total are not in the pack, so the script is inferred only from team form, not from a market number. Buffalo has been the more productive offense: James Cook 58 carries for 346 yards (5.97 YPC, 115.3 yards/game) and Josh Allen 23 carries for 119 yards in the same three games Dalton Kincaid posted 17 targets for 263 yards. New England allows 4.41 rush YPC and 10.53 YPA over the middle, and Drake Maye is -0.08 EPA/dropback overall and -0.23 versus blitz (n=29) against a Buffalo blitz rate of 31%. Base flow: Buffalo controls possession with a Cook run lean, still throws enough for Kincaid to work the middle, and New England is more likely to trail into dropbacks Maye has not graded well on.
script.flip1: New England hangs around or leads, Stevenson (31 carries, 116 yards L3) and Henderson (24 carries, 99 yards) keep the NE run game on the field, and Buffalo is forced pass-heavier. Cook's carries dip toward the mid-teens and 86.5 gets tight, while Kincaid's target count can rise.
script.flip2: Buffalo gets up big early and clocks it with Cook. Cook's rush over is helped, but pass volume shrinks so Kincaid can fall to 3 or fewer targets, and Allen's designed-run need drops even though he has averaged 39.7 rush yards on 23 L3 carries.

matchup.overlap: The core overlap is Dalton Kincaid (17 targets, 263 rec yards, 218 air yards) into the middle, where NE allows 10.53 YPA, plus James Cook (58 carries, 346 yards, 5.97 YPC) into a NE run defense allowing 4.41 YPC. NE's air-yard options (Hollins 194 air yards, Doubs 202) overlap BUF's 14 explosives allowed, but Maye's -0.23 EPA versus a 31% blitz cuts against that overlap.

data_check.notes: No projection, sim median, or Pinnacle no-vig is in the pack, so the test is L3 form versus the listed main lines. Cook's 115.3 rush-yard pace versus 86.5 is a 28.8-yard cushion. Applying NE's 4.41 YPC allowed to his 19.3-carry pace is about 85 yards, a close sizing caution, not a contradiction of the 115.3 actual. Kincaid's 87.7 receiving-yard pace versus 48.5 agrees. NE's 5 passes of 20+ on 99 attempts can trim his 15.5 yards per target, but the pack does not show the 263 yards were explosive-dependent. Allen rush over 31.5 (39.7 L3) and Coleman rec over 13.5 (33.7 L3) also clear their lines and were not selected. Stevenson rush over 32.5 (38.7 pace) is too thin in a trailing script. Henderson's 33.0 rush pace is under 40.5 but was left off to keep one Buffalo story. Cook over 86.5 is -114.5; Kincaid over 48.5 is +nan.

pre_mortem: It's Monday and both legs lost. Cook went under 86.5 because New England, with only 7 runs of 10+ allowed in three games, held him near the 4.41 YPC they allow and he never saw 18 carries: 16 carries at 4.4 YPC is about 70 yards, or Buffalo fell behind and passed. Kincaid went under 48.5 because NE's 5 explosives on 99 attempts and a middle bracket cut his 15.5 yards per target in half, and with Knox at 17 rec yards L3 and Shakir at 84 rec yards on 15 targets taking the checkdowns he finished near 4 targets for 35 yards. A late inactive would also void either read, and the pack has no injury report to rule that out. That efficiency counter-case is real but weaker than the role evidence (58 carries for 346 yards; 17 targets for 263 yards), so the legs stay, tied to those kill conditions.
slip_story: One Buffalo-offense story: Cook rush yards over 86.5 and Kincaid receiving yards over 48.5 were already produced together in the same L3 window (346 rush yards and 263 rec yards). They win if Buffalo controls the game the way the form says, Cook carrying against 4.41 YPC allowed and Kincaid working the middle against 10.53 YPA. They do not need NE overs such as Hollins (52.0 rec yards/game) or Doubs (48.3), which need Maye to beat a 31% blitz he has graded -0.23 EPA against. Do not add a total under or an NE rushing over; those need the opposite script.
